lines.text: A land of high mountains at the crossroads of Asia, where empires came and went and the Silk Road passed through. This is the story of Afghanistan.
In the west, Herat was already a city some two and a half thousand years ago. Much later it would shine as a centre of Timurid art and learning.
Around the time of Christ, the Kushans built an empire on the Silk Road. Their gold coins honoured many gods, and they helped Buddhism travel on to China.
In the Bamiyan valley, two giant Buddhas were carved into a sandstone cliff. They watched over the old road for some fifteen centuries.
In the tenth century a Turkish dynasty rose at Ghazni, and from there its armies raided deep into India.
In the 1190s, in a remote mountain valley, builders raised the Minaret of Jam, a tower of patterned brick that still stands.
Centuries later, in 1722, Ahmad Shah Durrani was born. He would unite the Afghan tribes under one crown.
In 1747 he was chosen as king, and the land took the shape of the country we call Afghanistan.
His Durrani Empire stretched far beyond today's borders, and is seen as the beginning of the modern Afghan state.
In 1776 the capital moved to Kabul, in a high valley of the Hindu Kush, and there it has stayed.
Then Britain and Russia began their contest for Central Asia, the Great Game. In 1839 a British army marched in, and by 1842 it had been wiped out.
Britain came back in 1878. This time it left Afghanistan's dealings with the outside world in British hands.
In 1892 Amanullah Khan was born. As king he would win full independence and try to bring the country into the modern age.
Mohammad Daoud Khan, born in 1909, would serve as prime minister, overthrow the monarchy and fall himself in a coup.
Zahir Shah, born in 1914, would be Afghanistan's last king, reigning for forty years.
In 1919, after a short war with Britain, Afghanistan took full control of its own affairs at last.
Ashraf Ghani was born in 1949. Decades later he would be president, until he fled as the Taliban took Kabul.
Ahmad Shah Massoud, born in 1953, became the commander who fought first the Soviets, then the Taliban.
Hamid Karzai, born in 1957, would lead the country after the Taliban fell in 2001.
In 1978 communists seized power in a coup, Daoud was killed, and Afghanistan's long years of war began.
The next year Soviet troops poured in to prop up the government. Rebels backed from abroad fought them for ten years, until the Soviets withdrew.
In the chaos that followed, a new Islamist movement emerged in 1994. The Taliban took Kabul two years later.
After the attacks of September 2001, the United States and its allies invaded and drove the Taliban from power. The war lasted twenty years.
In the summer of 2021, as the last American forces left, the Taliban swept back into Kabul.
And in October 2023 earthquakes struck near Herat, killing more than fourteen hundred people.
From the Buddhas of Bamiyan to the streets of Kabul, Afghanistan's people have endured it all.
